Con proposiciones y [[lg-conjuntos|conju: With propositions and [[lg-conjuntos|sets]] you can already make claims; this topic teaches you to know whether a claim is true without checking it in every case. The tools are the connectives from [[lg-proposiciones|logic]], especially implication and its contrapositive, and one new idea: the domino of induction.
Esto es lo que separa a las matemáticas: This is what separates mathematics from every other science. A physicist checks a law in a million experiments and takes it as good until something better comes along. A mathematician does not: either they prove it, and then it is true for ever and without exceptions, or they do not know.
<strong>Comprobar casos no demuestra nad: Checking cases proves nothing. However many examples work, there can always be one further on that does not. And it really happens, as you are about to see.

It reads, all chained together: “n even implies that n is two k, implies that n squared is four k squared, implies that n squared is even”.

That is a direct proof: start from the hypothesis and reach the conclusion by a chain of implications, with no gaps.

Se supone que la conclusión es <strong>f: You assume the conclusion is false and reason until you reach a contradiction. Since there can be no contradictions, the assumption was impossible and the conclusion had to be true.
Es el método con el que se demostraron d: It is the method with which two of the most famous results of Greek mathematics were proved: that the primes are infinite and that $\sqrt{2}$ cannot be written as a fraction. You will see both in full detail in the arithmetic block, which comes right afterwards; here only the shape of the reasoning matters.
Por si esa segunda frase te suena rara:: In case that second sentence sounds odd: saying that $\sqrt{2}$ cannot be written as a fraction means that there is no pair of integers whose quotient gives exactly that value, however hard you look. Such numbers are called irrational, and they have a topic of their own later on. What is astonishing —and what has to be proved— is that it is impossible, not simply that nobody has managed it.
Una reducción al absurdo entera: no hay: A complete proof by contradiction: there is no natural number greater than all of them
Queremos demostrar que <em>no existe un: We want to prove that there is no natural number greater than or equal to all the others. It is a negative claim —“there is no”— and those are the favourites of proof by contradiction.
<strong>Suponemos lo contrario</strong>:: We assume the opposite: that there does exist a natural number $M$ greater than or equal to every natural number.
Para razonar por absurdo, ¿qué es exacta: To reason by contradiction, what exactly do you have to assume?
Razonamos a partir de esa suposición: $M: We reason from that assumption: $M$ is natural, so $M + 1$ is too, and it is a natural number greater than $M$.
Si $M$ es natural, ¿qué otro natural pue: If $M$ is natural, what other natural number can you manufacture from it?
<strong>Contradicción</strong>: $M$ tení: Contradiction: $M$ was supposed to be greater than or equal to all of them, and we have just found a greater one. The two things cannot both be true.
Como la suposición lleva a un imposible,: Since the assumption leads to an impossibility, the assumption was false: no such $M$ exists. ∎
¿Qué se concluye cuando una suposición l: What do you conclude when an assumption leads to a contradiction?
La estructura es siempre la misma: supon: The structure is always the same: assume the opposite, reason normally, run into something impossible, and conclude. With $\sqrt{2}$ the collision takes a few more lines to arrive, but the skeleton is this one.
Para <strong>refutar</strong> una afirma: To refute a claim of the form “for all $x$…” no elaborate method is needed: it is enough to find a single case that fails. That is what the negation of a universal quantifier says.
La asimetría es total y conviene tenerla: The asymmetry is total and it is worth keeping in mind: proving a “for all” demands a general argument; refuting it demands only one example. That is why the first thing to do with a conjecture is to try to break it.
La reducción al absurdo es cómo se depur: Proof by contradiction is how you debug a program or locate a fault: “suppose the failure is in the network”; if something follows from that which does not match what you see, the failure is not in the network. And the contrapositive is the art of the tester: instead of checking that everything good happens, look for no bad case slipping through, which is the same claim seen from the other side.
¿Cómo se demuestra algo para <em>infinit: How do you prove something for infinitely many cases? Not by checking them one by one, obviously. Induction gives a way of doing it in two steps.

La imagen clásica es una fila infinita d: The classic image is an infinite row of dominoes. The base case says that the first one falls. The inductive step says that if one falls, it knocks over the next. With those two things, they all fall — and there is no need to push them one by one.
Si quitas el caso base pero dejas el pas: If you remove the base case but leave the inductive step, will any domino fall? And if you break the step at domino 5, how many fall: none, five, or all but the fifth?
Quita el caso base o rompe el paso induc: Remove the base case or break the inductive step and see what happens. Both are needed: neither is spare.

Induction does not stop at numbers. Anything defined by rules that name themselves admits the same reasoning, and from that come proofs about objects that cannot be numbered. The most useful case is programs: in [[len-gramatica|the machines and languages block]] a language is defined with seventeen rules, several of them recursive, and proving that every program translates correctly is exactly this: checking it in the base cases and assuming it true for the parts when proving it for the whole. It is called structural induction, and it is the same old induction with the objects ordered by size instead of the naturals.
La inducción se usaba de forma intuitiva: Induction had been used intuitively since ancient times, but it was Blaise Pascal who formulated it clearly around 1654, while studying his triangle. Curiously, he came to it through a wager: a professional gambler asked him how to split the money from an interrupted game, and from that correspondence between Pascal and Fermat the calculus of probabilities was also born. Two entire branches of mathematics came out of a casino question.
Cómo se escribe una demostración por ind: How a proof by induction is written
Vamos con el ejemplo canónico: la suma d: Here is the canonical example: the sum of the first $n$ natural numbers.
Demostrar por inducción que $1 + 2 + \\d: Prove by induction that $1 + 2 + \dots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ for every natural $n \ge 1$.
<strong>Caso base</strong> ($n = 1$): la: Base case ($n = 1$): the sum is $1$, and the formula gives $\frac{1\cdot 2}{2} = 1$. ✓
¿Cuál es el primer valor de $n$ que hay: What is the first value of $n$ you have to check, and what is the sum there?
<strong>Hipótesis de inducción</strong>:: Induction hypothesis: we assume the formula holds for some arbitrary $k$, $1 + \dots + k = \frac{k(k+1)}{2}$.
¿Qué se supone cierto en el paso inducti: What is assumed true in the inductive step?
<strong>Paso</strong>: queremos la suma: Step: we want the sum up to $k + 1$. It is the sum up to $k$ plus the new term, so we add $k + 1$ to both sides of the hypothesis: $1 + \dots + k + (k + 1) = \frac{k(k+1)}{2} + (k + 1)$.
¿Qué hay que añadir a la suma hasta $k$: What do you have to add to the sum up to $k$ to get the sum up to $k + 1$?
Operamos sacando factor común $(k + 1)$:: We work it out by taking out the common factor $(k + 1)$: $\frac{k(k+1)}{2} + (k + 1) = (k + 1)\left(\frac{k}{2} + 1\right) = \frac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}$.
Los dos sumandos tienen algo en común. ¿: The two terms have something in common. What factor can you take out?
Y eso es exactamente la fórmula con $n =: And that is exactly the formula with $n = k + 1$, because $\frac{(k+1)((k+1)+1)}{2} = \frac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}$. ∎
Fíjate en el paso 3: es el único sitio d: Notice step 3: it is the only place where the hypothesis is used. Without that use, there is no induction.
El paso clave es <em>usar la hipótesis</: The key step is using the hypothesis. If at no point in your proof by induction have you used that the formula holds for $k$, something is probably wrong.

You will see it applied in [[al-inversa]].
Con desigualdades, el paso inductivo tie: With inequalities the inductive step has a trick to it: you are not after an equality but after chaining estimates. To prove that $2^n > n$: if $2^k > k$, then $2^{k+1} = 2\cdot 2^k > 2k = k + k \ge k + 1$. Every inequality along the way has to be true, and the last one uses that $k \ge 1$.
La inducción es la recursión de los prog: Induction is the programmers' recursion written down: a base case and a rule that reduces the problem to the previous one. And it is what lets you trust a program nobody can test in full: the automatic metro on line 14 in Paris, or Airbus flight software, are not validated by testing every case —there are infinitely many— but by proving that the property is preserved step by step. A test finds errors; a proof by induction guarantees there are none.
Cien casos que funcionan no son una demo: A hundred cases that work are not a proof; a single case that fails is a refutation.
Sin él, el paso inductivo es una cadena: Without it, the inductive step is a chain of dominoes nobody pushes: none of them falls.
